candidates.title: Molecular basis for discrimination of cGAMP linkage isomers by a c-di-GMP-II riboswitch variant
candidates.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
candidates.journal_abbrev: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
candidates.authors: Xu X, Cheng W, You H, Hu Z, Bao X, Li H, Zhang J, Patel DJ, Ren A
candidates.abstract: Riboswitches are noncoding RNA regulatory motifs predominantly found in bacteria. Signaling molecules such as c-di-GMP, c-di-AMP, and 3′,3′-cGAMP have been reported to be recognized by riboswitches. In contrast, 2′,3′-cGAMP functions as a second messenger in mammalian cells, yet its interaction with RNA molecules remains unclear. Here, we report the crystal structures of a c-di-GMP-II riboswitch variant, c-di-GMP-II-Bh, bound to 2′,3′-cGAMP and 3′,3′-cGAMP. Both complexes adopt a similar overall RNA scaffold with an identical binding pocket composition. However, the ligand bases adopt inverted orientations in the binding pocket, resulting in distinct interaction patterns with residues A64 and G68 and differences in base-pair stacking against the phosphodiester backbone. Structural comparison together with ligand-binding assays of structure-guided mutants using isothermal titration calorimetry reveals the molecular principles by which an RNA riboswitch discriminates among cyclic dinucleotide linkage isomers, highlighting the remarkable sensitivity of RNA binding pockets to subtle ligand structural variations and provides a mechanistic framework for understanding ligand specificity in RNA–small molecule recognition.

candidates.title: Subpocket-Aware Fragment-Based Docking Pipeline for Kinase Ligand Design: Methodology and a PKA Case Study
candidates.journal: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
candidates.authors: Buchthal K, Kramer PL, Hubach D, Bach G, Wagner N, Krieger J, Klöpper M, Daude M, Diederich WE, Volkamer A
candidates.abstract: Protein kinases regulate signal transduction through phosphorylation, and their dysregulation drives diseases like cancer, autoimmune disorders, and Alzheimer’s, making them key drug targets. Fragment-based drug design offers a powerful route to kinase inhibitors but often neglects kinase-specific structural insights. While KinFragLib, a library consisting of 7486 fragments derived from kinase-ligand complexes, provides a rich resource, exhaustive recombination of its fragments is computationally demanding. Here, we present an efficient exploration strategy that integrates subpocket-guided fragment growing with template docking to navigate this vast chemical space. Our automated pipeline prioritizes kinase-specific structural information, enabling targeted generation of chemically diverse ligands. Applied to the PKA kinase, the approach produced 33758 candidate molecules with promising docking scores, of which 15 were synthesized. Seven molecules reduced kinase activity by more than 50% at an inhibitor concentration of 100 μM, and five of these compounds also showed promising efficacy at a concentration of 10 μM. The IC50 determination ultimately revealed that five of the molecules were effective in the two- to three-digit nanomolar range. Crystallographic validation confirmed the predicted binding mode of the most potent compound. This methodology demonstrates how structure-informed guidance can transform fragment-based design into a scalable route for discovering novel kinase inhibitors.

candidates.title: Structural basis of stepwise G protein activation by the viral chemokine receptor US28
candidates.authors: Jude KM, Suomivuori CM, Waghray D, Maeda S, Fujiyoshi Y, Inoue A, Garcia KC, Tsutsumi N
candidates.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) govern diverse cellular responses and are crucial drug targets. However, the sequence of structural events from G protein recognition to GDP release has remained elusive. Here, we leveraged the viral chemokine GPCR US28 to capture multiple activation states of the US28-Gq complex. Using cryo-electron microscopy and an engineered chemokine superagonist, we determined three distinct complex structures, capturing a GDP-bound Encounter state, the nucleotide-free Canonical state, and a putative intermediate bridging the two states, the Transition-to-Canonical state. These structures, along with simulations and functional data, provide high-resolution snapshots of a plausible G protein activation trajectory and support a stepwise conformational model for G protein activation. This activation cascade closely parallels mechanisms proposed for human GPCRs, suggesting a conserved GPCR signaling mechanism.

candidates.title: Structural basis of isoform-specific cAMP regulation and autoinhibition in hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channels
candidates.authors: Zorzini V, Kleiz-Ferreira J, Brams M, Gallardo R, De Gieter S, Kusch J, Ulens C
candidates.abstract: Hyperpolarization-activated, cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels generate rhythmic electrical activity in cardiac and neuronal tissues, with isoform-specific cyclic AMP (cAMP) sensitivity remaining poorly understood. While HCN2 exhibits strong cAMP regulation, HCN1 shows minimal response. To investigate the structural basis of this divergence, we analyzed two engineered HCN1 variants using cryo-electron microscopy. One variant (HCN112) incorporates the C-linker and cyclic nucleotide-binding domain from HCN2 into the HCN1 backbone and exhibited enhanced cAMP sensitivity, with structural analysis revealing a compressed cytoplasmic domain arrangement that may facilitate regulatory interactions. In contrast, the truncated HCN1ΔC variant (lacking the cytoplasmic domain) displayed an intermediately open pore conformation, supporting auto-inhibitory regulation by the cyclic nucleotide-binding domain in wild-type channels. These structural insights elucidate how domain-specific interactions modulate cAMP-dependent gating and intrinsic auto-inhibition, providing insights into questions about mechanistic divergence among HCN isoforms. Our findings not only shed new light on the structural mechanisms underlying isoform-specific cAMP sensitivity but also have implications for the development of therapeutic strategies targeting HCN channels in neurological and cardiac disorders.

candidates.title: The conserved bridging domain on HCV E1E2 glycoprotein complex is targeted by neutralizing antibodies from diverse lineages
candidates.authors: Chen F, Nguyen YTK, Lee YZ, Giang E, Lau SC, Koide Y, Hung SH, Ueno LA, He L, Toth EA, Fuerst TR, Lauer GM, Stanfield RL, Zhu J, Wilson IA, Law M
candidates.abstract: SUMMARYThe bridging domain (BD) region on hepatitis C virus (HCV) E1E2 glycoprotein complex is a conserved, E1-dependent conformational site of vulnerability formed by E2 residues 646–704. Given its importance for rational vaccine design, here, we characterized the genetic, structural, functional, and epitope features of 25 BD-directed nAbs isolated from HCV-infected individuals or immunized macaques. These antibodies derive from diverse B cell lineages but frequently display recurrent CDRH3 motifs and recognize overlapping epitopes spanning antigenic regions AR4 and AR5, with variable engagement of the E2 back layer (BL) region. A crystal structure of the macaque nAb RM3-26 bound to E2 core domain reveals a BL-directed binding mode analogous to the human nAb hcab40. Importantly, BD-directed nAbs achieve broad neutralization with minimal somatic hypermutation at contact residues and act additively with neutralizing face-directed antibodies. Together, these findings underscore BD as a promising target for rational HCV vaccine design.

candidates.abstract: SignificanceWe demonstrate the existence and unique structural properties of the Extraordinarily Intricate Globular Helical Tangled fold—proteins likely containing one of the most complex knots identified in nature to date, an 83 knot. This previously uncharacterized topology was predicted de novo by AlphaFold without using template structures. The EIGHT fold structure occurs only in certain gut bacteria and exhibits unusual symmetry, likely from duplication of a simpler ancestor. In silico and in vitro analyses reveal unfolding through six distinct phases, spanning milliseconds to days. Native contacts allow the EIGHT fold to self-tie, but the observed folding pathway cannot be explained by any known protein-folding theory.

candidates.authors: Goncalves MM, Uday AB, Watson IDG, Chau AM, Kalhor-Monfared S, Wan B, Kiyota T, Currie SQW, Jitkova Y, Feng Y, Diamandas M, Ling D, Ma M, Mancini RS, Wang Z, Casás-Selves M, Joshi D, Mohammed M, Subramaniam R, Fernandes EL, Yan Y, Pomroy N, Hurren R, Gronda M, Velyvis A, Yudin AK, Reed MA, Prive G, Aman A, Isaac M
candidates.abstract: ClpP protease maintains proteostasis in human mitochondria and is overexpressed in cancers such as acute myeloid leukemia (AML). While activators such as dordaviprone (ONC201) have reached the clinic, the development of ClpP inhibitors has been hampered by paradoxical activation upon orthosteric inhibitor binding. Here, we report a series of quinazolinone-based compounds that allosterically inhibit human ClpP with nanomolar potency. Cryo-EM and H/D exchange mass spectrometry reveal that our lead compound binds sub-stoichiometrically to a distal hydrophobic pocket ~30 Å from the active sites, disrupts a conserved inter-subunit cluster, and induces a conformational change that misaligns the catalytic triad, thereby inactivating ClpP. The binding site of our quinazolinone-based inhibitors partially overlaps with that of the activator dordaviprone. In a xenograft mouse model of leukemia, our lead compound significantly reduced tumor burden following short-term oral administration. Our findings identify a regulatory hotspot in human ClpP and a mechanistically distinct inhibition strategy.

candidates.authors: Kandola TK, Mycroft-West CJ, Lima MA, Turner A, Gardini C, Urso E, Torode TA, Miller GJ, Bisio A, Yates EA, Guerrini M, Skidmore MA, Wu L
candidates.abstract: AbstractHeparin is a sulfated glycosaminoglycan, and the most used pharmaceutical anticoagulant worldwide. Heparin is isolated primarily from porcine sources, and possesses a complex variable structure, wherein anticoagulant activity is principally derived from the pentasaccharide GlcNS6S-GlcA-GlcNS3S6S-IdoA2S-GlcNS6S (AGA*IA) motif, containing an infrequent 3-O-sulfated glucosamine that enhances antithrombin stabilization. Pedobacter heparinus heparin lyases are currently widely employed for characterization of heparin and its derivatives, but have limited activity near regions of 3-O-sulfation, hindering analyses of anticoagulation relevant sequences. Here, using a panel of biophysical and structural techniques, we show that Bacteroides eggerthii lyase I liberates ΔUA-GlcNS3S6S disaccharides from the defined pentasaccharide, fondaparinux. This activity provides improved access to 3-O-sulfated heparin standards, with potential to aid heparin quality control.

candidates.title: Structural insights into peptidoglycan hydrolysis by the FtsEX system in Escherichia coli during cell division
candidates.authors: Li J, He Y, Xu X, Alcorlo M, Shi J, Naskar S, Briggs NS, Roper DI, Hermoso JA, Sham LT, Luo M
candidates.abstract: Bacterial cell division relies on precise peptidoglycan (PG) remodeling, a process orchestrated by the FtsEX complex. Comprised of FtsE and FtsX, this complex collaborates with EnvC, a periplasmic lytic enzyme activator, to regulate septal PG hydrolysis by amidases like AmiB. While recent structural investigations, particularly of Pseudomonas aeruginosa FtsEX (PaeFtsEX), have shed light on complex interactions and proposed activation mechanisms, the structural intricacies governing PG degradation by the FtsEX complex and EnvC in Escherichia coli cytokinesis remain unexplored. In this study, we present a comprehensive biochemical and structural analysis of E. coli FtsEX complexes, unveiling a key role for ATP in complex stabilization that extends across bacterial species. Upon EnvC binding, ATPase activity markedly increases. High-resolution structures of EcoFtsEX, both in the presence and absence of EnvC, reveal a symmetrical conformation of EcoFtsEX capable of accommodating the inherent asymmetry of EnvC, mediated by flexible loops within the periplasmic domain. Our negative-staining imaging showcases an elongated EcoFtsEX/EnvC/AmiB complex reminiscent of the PaeFtsEX system. These findings collectively provide intricate insights into the regulation of PG cleavage by FtsEX in E. coli—a pivotal model system used in pilot genetic studies, suggesting a conserved mechanism for precise hydrolase activation in bacteria.

candidates.title: A Cytosine‑Bulged (3+1) Hybrid G‑Quadruplex Formed by the Chicken DNA Replication Origin
candidates.authors: You Y, Suen MC, Miao H, Geng Y, Din RU, Yuan M, Xue Q, Li X, Xu N, Guo Z, Lam H, Lo K, Liu C, Zhu G
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTGuanine (G)‐rich nucleic acid sequences, capable of folding into G‐quadruplex (G4), are widely distributed in functionally important genomic regions and play key roles in DNA replication. Origin G‐rich repeated elements (OGRE) have been identified at replication origins in mouse, Drosophila, human and chicken. However, G4 structures formed by OGRE remain poorly understood. Here, we report the first high‑resolution G4 structure formed by OGRE from the β‐globin replication origin of chicken (Gallus gallus). The 23 nt DNA sequence d[GGGAACGCGGCATCAGGGTGGGG], termed ChOGRE23, folds into an intramolecular three‐layer (3+1) hybrid G4 containing a cytosine bulge. Notably, the 5'‐end guanine participating in the outermost G‐quartet adopts an anti glycosidic conformation, representing a previously unobserved glycosidic alignment in unimolecular (3+1) hybrid G4s. Together with the cytosine bulge, these unusual structural features create a distinct molecular surface that may facilitate selective recognition by replication‑associated proteins or small molecules.

candidates.title: Induced-fit anti-GFRAL antibody ameliorates cancer cachexia and attenuates sympathetic outflow in tumor-bearing mice
candidates.authors: Kim S, Lee MH, Ahn J, Ju SH, Lee DS, Choi S, Min KW, Shong M, Kim HM
candidates.abstract: The GDF15–GFRAL–RET neuroendocrine axis is a key regulator of body-weight homeostasis and metabolic control. GFRAL, a hindbrain-restricted receptor for the stress-responsive cytokine GDF15, signals by assembling a ternary complex with GDF15 and the tyrosine kinase RET. Pathological hyperactivation of this axis drives disease-associated weight loss, including cancer-associated cachexia. Here, we report a GFRAL-binding and GDF15–GFRAL pathway-blocking antibody (GB2Ab) and its humanized lead with potent preclinical efficacy. The GB2Ab Fab–GFRAL D3 crystal structure reveals an induced-fit mechanism in which GB2Ab sterically occludes the GFRAL–RET interface and remodels the primary RET CLD1–CLD2 binding site, providing a structural basis for high-affinity binding, slow dissociation, and potent antagonism. Structure-guided humanization preserves high-affinity and cross-reactivity. The humanized antibody reaches the area postrema, attenuates GDF15-evoked neural activation, ameliorates cachectic phenotypes, and suppresses sympathetic preganglionic activity in an orthotopic cancer cachexia model, establishing receptor-centric GDF15–GFRAL–RET antagonism as a promising strategy for cancer-associated cachexia and other GDF15-driven diseases.

candidates.title: Structural and biophysical studies of human E3 ligase Deltex 4
candidates.authors: Fowkes MM, Elkins JM
candidates.abstract: AbstractDeltex (DTX) E3 ligases such as DTX1 and DTX2 are known to bind to ADP-ribosylated substrates and consequently ubiquitinate them. However, little is known about the role of the DTX E3 ligase DTX4 in substrate binding and ubiquitination. Here, we present the crystal structure of the DTX4 RING-DTC domains in complex with ADP-ribose to a final resolution of 2.8 Å and uncover a unique domain swap within the RING domain. Structural comparison with the closely related RING-DTC domains of DTX1 and DTX2 reveals similarities but also differences in the mode of ligand binding and the number and type of conserved residues. Biophysical assays to assess the strength of binding to nucleotide units of poly-ADP-ribose (PAR) demonstrate a preference for binding to ADP-ribose, strengthening existing evidence for PAR binding. Collectively, the structural and binding data offer insights into the active structure of DTX4 and its interaction with nucleotide units of PAR.

candidates.abstract: The large protein (L) of nonsegmented, negative-strand RNA viruses, a viral order that includes rabies, Ebola, Nipah, and respiratory syncytial viruses, catalyze RNA-dependent RNA polymerization on nucleocapsid-sheathed RNA templates. L coordinates two distinct processes: messenger RNA (mRNA) transcription and genome replication. During transcription, L catalyzes cotranscriptional mRNA capping, methylation, and polyadenylation. The additional activities are not required during genome replication; instead, RNA synthesis is coupled to encapsidation by soluble nucleoprotein (N0) recruited by the phosphoprotein (P). We determined the structure of a vesicular stomatitis virus polymerase complex comprising L-P and N0. P directly engages the carboxyl-terminal domain of L (LCTD) to anchor N0 in a continuum of conformations including a more stable configuration with N0 positioned at the RNA-product exit channel, poised for encapsidation. This study reveals a function for LCTD in encapsidation of nascent RNAs and provides the structure of a polymerase complex required for genomic RNA replication.

candidates.authors: Bütikofer M, Torres F, Ghosh D, Lorz N, Riek R, Orts J
candidates.abstract: Phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (PGK1) is a key metabolic enzyme responsible for ATP production, and its dysregulation is linked to the Warburg effect in cancer and to neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s. candidates.title: Building a Physically Interpretable Compressed Chemical Space via Grid-Based Optimization
candidates.journal: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
candidates.authors: Yoon S, Dickson A
candidates.abstract: In recent years, deep generative models have been increasingly adopted for molecular optimization and design. In many such models, molecules are encoded into latent spaces that provide compact representations of their features. However, these latent spaces remain difficult to interpret in physical terms, and it is unclear how much structural and molecular information is retained under compression. This limitation becomes especially important when molecular behavior depends on specific three-dimensional arrangements embedded in an environmental context. Here, we introduce COMPRESS (Compression Of Molecular Physical fields into Reduced Spatial Sites), an optimization framework that represents a small molecule using a fixed number of physically parametrized spatial sites. Each site is defined by three spatial coordinates and three interaction parameters, yielding a fixed-size representation that remains directly interpretable in physical terms. To preserve molecular information, COMPRESS representations are optimized to reproduce the density, electrostatic, and van der Waals fields of the corresponding all-atom molecule on discretized three-dimensional grids. We systematically evaluate how molecular information is retained as the number of sites, K, is reduced. Our analysis covers benzene, 20 chemically diverse chemical scaffolds, benzene dimers, protein–ligand complexes, and 10,000 molecules chosen from the GEOM-Drugs data set. Across systems, field agreement deteriorates slowly at high resolution and then undergoes a rapid, pronounced transition at lower resolution. We further find that K = 25 conformers capture about 97% of the molecules from GEOM-Drugs under a loss threshold of 0.05, which we use as an indicator of fidelity. These results show that COMPRESS can provide a fixed-size, physically interpretable molecular representation, enabling compression to be evaluated directly using molecular interaction fields and resulting physical quantities. We also introduce a decoder that reconstructs all-atom structures directly from a COMPRESS representation, showing that the representation can support molecular generation in addition to field-preservation analysis. Finally, rationally modified COMPRESS representations through changes to site charge and size or the addition or removal of sites are shown to generate realistic chemical compounds upon decoding.

candidates.abstract: Chronic cadmium (Cd) exposure, even in environmental conditions, has been associated with metabolic disorders such as dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes. Isolated islets showed exaggerated second-phase insulin release and increased Ki-67 with reduced Bcl-2 immunoreactivity, suggesting compensatory β-cell proliferation under subtoxic stress. Spectroscopic and theoretical analyses support the possibility that Cd²⁺ substitutes Zn²⁺ within insulin coordination sites, leading to structural perturbations. In vivo, insulin–Cd conjugates exhibited diminished hypoglycemic efficacy despite elevated circulating insulin levels, indicating reduced bioactivity. candidates.abstract: AbstractHeme serves as a crucial cofactor for hemoproteins and as an iron reservoir; yet, its accumulation is toxic, necessitating efficient degradation pathways. Moreover, we show that the degradation of heme c by the Core‐only‐type HOs requires proteolytic digestion of heme c‐carrying proteins by a protease such as DegQ, which occurs in the periplasm. candidates.abstract: Bis-FeIV-forming enzymes represent an emerging paradigm in high-valent heme iron chemistry, in which two hemes separated by 15–20 Å are both oxidized to the FeIV state. Computational pathway analysis identified the possibility of an alternative, non-covalent route mediated by Arg283 and a heme propionate with possible electronic coupling comparable to the native tryptophan pathway. Consistent with this prediction, only simultaneous disruption of both the tryptophan and propionate-mediated pathways abolished bis-FeIV formation entirely. Moreover, only mutants capable of forming bis-FeIV retained the ability to turnover substrate, directly establishing this high-valent state as the catalytic intermediate responsible for substrate modification. These results demonstrate that an intervening tryptophan is not required for fast inter-heme electron transfer, and instead reveal an additional, non-covalent pathway that may be a general feature of diheme peroxidases.

candidates.title: Harnessing marine polysaccharides for breast cancer therapy: ulvan synergizes with nano-selenium to induce programmed cell death through dual modulation of autophagy and apoptosis
candidates.authors: Mekkawy SA, Abdelmaguid AM, El-Khadragy MF, Aly AA, Abdelfattah MS, Abdalla MS
candidates.abstract: BackgroundSince breast cancer is one of the biggest worldwide health issues, new and effective treatment approaches are required. Because autophagy control has two context-dependent roles in the development of cancer, it is a prospective therapeutic target. With an emphasis on the regulation of oxidative stress, inflammation, apoptosis, and autophagy, this work assessed the anticancer potential of ulvan, a sulfated polysaccharide produced from Ulva lactuca, and ulvan-loaded nano-selenium in an Ehrlich solid carcinoma model.MaterialESC-bearing mice were treated with ulvan extract, sodium selenite or ulvan-SeNPs for 14 days. The anticancer activity was assessed through histology, oxidative stress markers, inflammatory mediators, apoptotic proteins and genes expression for autophagy and molecular docking studies.ResultsMolecular docking analysis revealed ulvan-derived saccharides to bind strongly to VEGFR2, CD44 and Toll-like receptors suggesting multi-target action. Ulvan in vivo restored antioxidant defenses, reduced oxidative stress and inflammatory markers and induced apoptosis via caspase-3, Bcl-2 and Bax modulation. Ulvan induced controlled autophagy by decreasing mTOR and increasing autophagy related gene expression. Ulvan-SeNPs exhibited enhanced anticancer activity with increased activation of autophagic and apoptotic pathways, as evidenced by tumor shrinkage, reduced angiogenesis and histopathological analysis.ConclusionUlvan is a controlled anti-cancer agent, with a mechanism synergistically enhanced by nano-selenium. These results indicate that ulvan could be a potential natural therapeutic for breast cancer alone or in combination with nano-selenium.

candidates.title: Identification and functional validation of lactylation-related hub genes in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis based on multi-omics analysis
candidates.authors: Yue M, Luan R, Ding D, Hu X, Tan J, Zhao M, Zhu L, Xue Q, Yang J
candidates.abstract: BackgroundIdiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive, irreversible interstitial lung disease (ILD) characterized by high mortality and poorly understood pathogenesis. Lactylation, a recently identified post-translational modification (PTM), is closely associated with inflammatory responses and tissue fibrosis in various diseases. However, the expression patterns and potential roles of lactylation, as well as the key regulatory genes involved, have not been fully elucidated in IPF. This study aimed to identify lactylation-related hub genes in IPF through bioinformatics analysis and preliminary functional validation, to explore their therapeutic potential, and to evaluate their binding affinity with clinical drugs, providing a theoretical basis for future research on lactylation mechanisms and targeted interventions in IPF.MethodsTranscriptomic and single-cell sequencing datasets from lung tissues of IPF patients and healthy controls (HC) were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) was performed to identify IPF-related gene modules. Lactylation-associated hub genes were determined by integrating lactylation-related gene sets with protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis. Seurat software and UMAP clustering were employed to identify cell-specific localization of hub genes in lung tissues. Preliminary functional validations, including immunohistochemistry (IHC), Western blotting (WB) for pan-lactylation detection, and gene knockdown assays, were conducted in vitro and in vivo. The CIBERSORT algorithm was applied to analyze immune cell infiltration profiles in IPF tissues. Molecular docking analyses were performed to assess the binding affinity of clinical antifibrotic drugs (pirfenidone and curcumin) with proteins encoded by hub genes.ResultsDDX3X, BCLAF1, and NCL were identified as lactylation-related hub genes in IPF and were specifically expressed in macrophages/neutrophils, ciliated epithelial cells, and lung fibroblasts/macrophages, respectively. The level of pan-lactylation was significantly elevated in IPF lung tissues and TGF-β1-stimulated cellular models. These three hub genes were significantly upregulated in IPF tissues compared with HC, and individual knockdown of each gene significantly inhibited alveolar epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and human fetal lung fibroblast (HFL1) activation. In addition, these hub genes were closely associated with immune microenvironment remodeling in IPF. Pirfenidone and curcumin demonstrated favorable binding affinity with the proteins encoded by these genes.ConclusionThe lactylation-related hub genes DDX3X, BCLAF1, and NCL are specifically expressed in distinct cell types within IPF lung tissues, and their upregulation may promote IPF progression by mediating alveolar epithelial EMT, fibroblast activation, and profibrotic immune infiltration, highlighting their potential as therapeutic targets for IPF. Aberrant lactylation activation may contribute to IPF pathogenesis. Pirfenidone and curcumin show promising binding affinity with these hub gene-encoded proteins, providing a theoretical basis for further investigation into lactylation-targeted therapeutic strategies in IPF.Graphical Abstract Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12931-026-03783-3.

candidates.abstract: The RAF–MEK–ERK signaling pathway plays a central role in cancer development and progression and represents an important target for anticancer drug discovery. Simultaneous targeting of components of this pathway may therefore represent a promising strategy for cancer treatment. A quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) model was developed using multiple linear regression (MLR). The QSAR model showed satisfactory predictive performance based on complementary internal and external validation metrics. The selected molecular descriptors were used to guide the structural modification of substituents, resulting in higher predicted activity. Accordingly, ten new molecules were designed through strategic substituent modifications. Synthetic routes for these compounds were also proposed based on reported literature procedures. Molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and Petra, Osiris, and Molinspiration (POM) analyses supported the prioritization of Pred 9 and Pred 10 as computationally designed candidates for further investigation. In silico absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) predictions indicated that Pred 9 and Pred 10 may exhibit favorable pharmacokinetic properties. Overall, the results support the consideration of these compounds for experimental synthesis and biological evaluation. However, Pred 9 and Pred 10 have not yet been synthesized or experimentally evaluated for MEK1 inhibition or anticancer activity.

candidates.title: MICA Allelic Variation Modulates Secretion and Protein Flexibility, Impacting on NKG2D‐Mediated Immune Responses and Antibody Detection
candidates.authors: López‐Borrego S, Toledo‐Stuardo K, Matthies DJ, González‐Matesanz M, Molina MC, Valés‐Gómez M
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTNKG2D is an essential receptor for cancer immunosurveillance, activating Natural Killer (NK) and CD8+ T‐cells to eliminate transformed cells. However, release of its ligands promotes immune evasion. Although new therapeutic strategies aim to block NKG2D‐ligand shedding, the impact of allelic polymorphism on secretion mechanisms, either as soluble proteins or within extracellular vesicles (EVs), remains insufficiently explored. The glycosyl–phosphatidyl–inositol (GPI)‐anchored MICA (MHC class I chain‐related gene A) *008 allele is preferentially incorporated into EVs, but little is known about the EV release of other alleles. Here, we compared five MICA alleles and found that non‐GPI‐MICA can also be incorporated into EVs through a palmitoylation‐dependent process, although with much lower efficiency compared with GPI‐anchored alleles, such as MICA*008. EVs containing MICA decreased NKG2D detection and impaired NK cell function, whereas soluble MICA had negligible effects. The strength of these effects was related to MICA allele identity. In addition to affinity (ruled by dimorphism at position 129), predictions of differences in MICA structural dynamics and NKG2D binding energetics coincided with the differential capacity of alleles to modulate NKG2D and to bind certain anti‐MICA antibodies. Given the clinical potential of MICA as a biomarker and therapeutic target, defining the biology and immune impact of allelic variants is essential to optimize strategies aimed at restoring NKG2D‐dependent antitumor immunity.

candidates.title: Mapping Functional Transitions across Protein Homologues from a Single Simulation: Application of gEDES-HM to Adenylate Kinases
candidates.journal: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
candidates.authors: Kurt H, Athar M, Basciu A, Reys V, Bonvin AMJJ, Vargiu AV
candidates.abstract: Proteins fluctuate across different conformational states, which constitute a dynamic ensemble that regulates their interaction networks and functions. Predicting the conformational landscape remains a computational challenge, and even more difficult is capturing the link between state distributions and specific functions within protein homologues. Here, we present gEDES-HM (generalized Ensemble Docking with Enhanced sampling of pocket Shape-Homology Modeling), a scalable computational protocol enabling us to remap conformational ensembles obtained from enhanced sampling simulations of a single protein to its homologous family members, removing the need to perform individual simulations for all of them and thus speeding up the whole process by orders of magnitude. Specifically, we exploit our recent gEDES protocol to bias through metadynamics simulations the shape and volume of the binding site(s) of a reference protein. Next, a number of maximally diverse conformations of the protein are extracted from a multistep cluster analysis and used together as a multitemplate library for comparative modeling of the conformational ensemble of each homologue in the pool. This enables the functional conformational ensemble of one protein to be transferred to its homologues and used, for example, in restrained ensemble docking. We validated the protocol on 22 homologues of the E. coli adenylate kinase (hereafter, ADK), corresponding to 26 protein-ligand complexes and spanning 31% to 99% sequence identity to the reference. Our protocol retrieves a bound-like conformation of the protein binding site (corresponding to experimental substrate/inhibitor-bound states) for almost all targets, which allows reproducing native-like binding modes for 92% of the investigated complexes in ensemble docking calculations. Validated so far within a single family, gEDES-HM could provide a practical route to generate binding-competent structural libraries for homologues lacking experimental structures suitable for downstream structure-based modeling.

candidates.title: Membranes Decouple α‑Synuclein Surface Assembly and Kinetic Restriction from Persistent Amyloid-like Intermolecular Organization
candidates.authors: Chen J, Chu X
candidates.abstract: Membrane association places α-synuclein (αSyn) at the boundary between physiological surface organization and pathological amyloid assembly, supporting vesicle clustering, surface condensation, and amyloid nucleation. How interfacial recruitment, condensate cohesion, and persistent amyloid-like organization are coupled or decoupled remains unclear. Because membrane binding also induces helical ordering in the N-terminal membrane-binding region and the aggregation-prone non-amyloid-β component (NAC) region, we used multichain coarse-grained simulations to separate conformational ordering from recruitment by an anionic POPC/POPG bilayer. Helical/ordered segments promoted locally dense, directionally packed assemblies but weakened global condensate cohesion. Membrane association produced flattened surface assemblies and increased the protein population outside the largest condensate. Despite becoming dynamically restricted, these membrane-associated condensates did not show systematically prolonged NAC contact lifetimes. Thus, membrane-driven surface assembly and kinetic restriction can be decoupled from persistent amyloid-like intermolecular organization, explaining how lipid interfaces promote αSyn clustering without necessarily driving amyloid-competent organization.

candidates.authors: Phan UT, Lee JM, Vo TM, Oh MK, Kim YH
candidates.abstract: Tungsten-dependent formate dehydrogenases are among the most active biological catalysts for carbon dioxide reduction, but their production is limited by complex metal cofactor requirements and poor compatibility with standard expression hosts. Here, we address this limitation by engineering an Escherichia coli chassis through reconstruction of tungsten cofactor biosynthesis, installation of a high-affinity tungstate transporter, and reinforcement of iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis. The resulting chassis produces the formate dehydrogenase from Methylorubrum extorquens with native-level specific activity, near-stoichiometric tungsten incorporation, and high volumetric activity, while substantially enhancing whole-cell CO-driven CO₂-to-formate conversion compared with the native-host system. The engineered host demonstrates broad applicability by supporting maturation of tungsten-dependent formate dehydrogenases from Cupriavidus necator, Lutibaculum baratangense, Thermococcus onnurineus, and Thermoanaerobacter kivui. In this work, we show that engineering host metal cofactor metabolism provides a strategy for aerobic production of active tungsten-dependent formate dehydrogenases, expanding access to this enzyme family for biological and biotechnological applications.

candidates.title: NEK1 autophosphorylation is disrupted by amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated missense variants: activity biomarkers and structural insights
candidates.authors: Agarwal S, Rehman SAA, Muñoz IM, Knebel A, Hop PJ, Gourlay R, Brown F, Macartney T, Squires I, Veldink JH, Kenna KP, Rouse J, Mehta AR
candidates.abstract: AbstractRare variants in NEK1, encoding a serine/threonine kinase, are among the most consistently implicated genetic contributors to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), reported in approximately 2–3% of cases. Yet, while recent studies have characterized the cell biological consequences of NEK1 loss-of-function, the biochemical effects of ALS-associated missense variants on kinase activity have not been directly investigated. This distinction is mechanistically important, because missense alleles encode mutant proteins rather than simply reducing protein dosage. Here, we provide the most comprehensive cell-based phosphoproteomic map of NEK1 phosphorylation to date, identifying 10 recurrent phosphorylation sites across independent expression and acquisition conditions. We experimentally assign pSer14, pThr156 and pSer418 as NEK1 autophosphorylation sites using kinase-dead controls, targeted extracted ion chromatogram analysis, phosphosite mutagenesis and phosphospecific antibodies. Leveraging activation-loop pThr156 as a read-out of NEK1 activity, we assessed nine ALS-associated missense variants spanning the major functional regions of the protein. Among catalytic-domain variants, R261C produced the most robust reduction in pThr156 autophosphorylation, R232C produced a smaller reduction, and R232H increased pThr156; the basic-region variant, A313T, also showed a smaller reduction. Structural modelling provides a mechanistic framework for understanding these variant-specific effects. Our study establishes the first activity-based framework for functional classification of NEK1 missense variants, and provides direct evidence that ALS-associated missense variants can alter NEK1 autophosphorylation through a mechanism distinct from simple haploinsufficiency. The phosphospecific antibodies, isogenic cell lines and curated phosphoproteomic datasets generated here provide a community resource for future studies of NEK1 regulation, variant interpretation and therapeutic target validation.

candidates.title: New thiazole/coumarin hybrids as EGFR inhibitors with potential VEGFR-2 inhibition (design, synthesis, biological evaluation, and dynamic stimulation)
candidates.authors: Elshemy SW, Ali TFS, Sayed AM, Abbas SH
candidates.abstract: Two new series of coumarin–thiazole hybrids (6a–i and 9a–h) were designed and synthesized as EGFR/VEGFR-2 dual inhibitors. Hybrids 6a–i demonstrated remarkable antiproliferative activities on different NCI-60 cell lines in a single-dose assay. The antiproliferative activities of the newly synthesized hybrids were evaluated against a panel of three human cancer cell lines (HepG2, HCT-116, and MCF-7). Compounds 6a, 6h, 9a, and 9d were the four most active hybrids. Herein, compound 6a was the most active antiproliferative agent among the 6a–i hybrids, with IC50 values ranging from 2.85 µM to 7.66 µM. At the same time, compound 9d was the most active antiproliferative agent among the 9a–h hybrids, with IC50 values ranging from 3.79 µM to 9.80 µM. Furthermore, hybrids 6a, 6h, 9a, and 9d expressed low cytotoxicity for the normal fetal lung WI-38 cells. Consistent with the mechanistic study, the most potent compounds (6a, 6h, and 9d) displayed remarkable inhibitory effectiveness against EGFR and VEGFR-2. Moreover, the most potent hybrid (6a) caused the upregulation of Bax, cytochrome c, and caspase-3 levels and downregulation of Bcl-2 levels. Molecular docking study for compounds 6a, 6h, 9a, and 9d agreed with the mechanistic results. Molecular docking into the ATP-binding site of EGFR (PDB: 1M17 and re-docking RMSD = 1.43 Å) and VEGFR-2 (PDB: 4ASD and re-docking RMSD = 1.67 Å) confirmed strong binding affinities for 6a (ΔG = −10.32 and −9.98 kcal mol−1, respectively) and 9d (ΔG = −10.23 and −9.87 kcal mol−1, respectively), consistent with their enzymatic inhibition profiles. To validate the dynamic stability of binding, 100 ns all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed for 6a and 9d in complex with EGFR, alongside erlotinib and the apo receptor. Compound 6a was carried forward into the 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of five systems, comprising the apo receptor, the erlotinib complex and the complexes of 6a, 9d, and 9a. Ligand binding compacted the kinase by roughly 2.3 Å in the radius of gyration relative to the apo receptor and reduced Cα fluctuation across the fold. The total protein–ligand interaction energy ranked the four ligands in an order consistent with the enzymatic assay, yielding values of −69.6, −55.6, −50.6 and −41.7 kcal mol−1 for erlotinib, 6a, 9d and 9a against IC50 values of 0.14, 0.27, 0.378, and 2.94 µM, respectively. Furthermore, every pairwise separation exceeded twice the block-averaged standard error. Compound 6a was identified as the lead compound of the series.

candidates.title: Nonadditive Conformational Effects of tRNA Core Modifications
candidates.journal: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
candidates.authors: Amissah TE, Levintov L, Vashisth H
candidates.abstract: Post-transcriptional modifications are known to regulate the structure and function of tRNA molecules. Compared to modifications in the anticodon region, the mechanistic effects of modifications in the core region of tRNA remain poorly understood. Using all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on yeast tRNAPhe, we investigated the conformational effects of incorporating chemical modifications in the core region (termed hereafter “core modifications”) of tRNA. Specifically, we focused on three core modifications, namely, 7-methylguanosine (m7G), 5-methylcytosine (m5C), and 1-methyladenosine (m1A). We discovered that individual modifications increased the structural stability of tRNA, but their combinations produced multimodal free energy landscapes with multiple distinct basins. We identified m1A58 as a bifunctional regulator that locally disrupts structure while globally coordinating anticorrelated arm movement. The combination of m1A58 and m5C49 exhibited the lowest structural deviation from the crystal structure, while the triply modified variant incorporating all three modifications produced the most integrated residue community network, reflecting nonadditive allosteric coupling that cannot be predicted from any pairwise combination. Critically, core modifications established extensive allosteric pathways that prevent the consistent inward displacement of the anticodon stem loop otherwise observed in all simulations of chemically unmodified tRNA. Our results demonstrate that core modifications function as regulators of conformational ensembles rather than simple stabilizers.

candidates.title: PDI-Spot: A Robust Representation Learning Framework for Identifying Energetic Hotspots in Protein–DNA Complexes
candidates.journal: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
candidates.authors: Basaran E, Gursoy A, Keskin O, Tuncbag N
candidates.abstract: The binding affinity of protein–DNA complexes is concentrated within a subset of interface residues, called “hotspots”, which are critical for maintaining stable interactions. Therefore, identifying these energetic anchors is essential for elaborating on how mutations disrupt transcriptional regulation and for identifying druggable regions within disease-associated interfaces. In this study, we introduce our novel prediction model, PDI-Spot, that leverages representation learning to capture the complex features of protein–DNA interfaces. Unlike traditional methods that rely on limited, handcrafted descriptors, PDI-Spot extracts high-dimensional, structure- and sequence-driven representations to achieve better predictive performance. We trained the PDI-Spot model on a curated protein–DNA complex data set and rigorously validated its performance on an independent test set to ensure generalizability across different structural families. Following the extraction of residue-level embeddings, an optimal feature set was identified through a combined approach of minimum redundancy maximum relevance and multilayer perceptron architectures. By training a neural network on the optimal feature set, we developed a robust predictive framework for hotspot identification. On an independent test set, PDI-Spot achieved an AUROC of 0.809, an F1-score of 0.667, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.625. We also verified via permutation tests that PDI-Spot captures biologically meaningful patterns beyond random chance. PDI-Spot consistently demonstrates competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, providing a reliable model for mapping the energetic landscapes of protein–DNA interfaces. The source code and pretrained models are publicly available at https://github.com/ebsrn0/pdi-spot.git.

candidates.authors: Li S, He W, Zhang M, Zhang X, Fang WQ, Xu MJ, Shi Y, Cai Y, Zhang Y, Da LT
candidates.abstract: Specific recognition between proteins and DNA governs essential cellular functions, yet the binding specificity of most DNA-binding proteins (DBPs) remains experimentally uncharacterized and high-throughput experimental methods still lag far behind the ever-growing protein data set. candidates.title: Spatiotemporally stratified nanoassemblies for precisely halting the immunothrombotic vicious cycle in acute lung inflammation
candidates.authors: Li C, Ni Y, Huang J, Li J, Zheng Y, Zhang Y, Cao L, Wang Z, Chen L
candidates.abstract: Acute lung injury and acute respiratory distress syndrome have high mortality. Extensive pulmonary microvascular thrombosis occurs in over 80% of patients who die from severe pneumonia. Inflammation and thrombosis mutually aggravate each other, forming a vicious cycle that accelerates disease progression. Nevertheless, it remains challenging to achieve safe and balanced anti-inflammatory treatment and systemic anticoagulation. These two pathological processes are spatially separated, coagulation arises on the vascular endothelial surface, while inflammatory signals are confined inside immune cells. Current therapeutic strategies fail to realize simultaneous and precise dual regulation within a single delivery system. Therefore, we developed a spatiotemporally hierarchical responsive nanoplatform called Hep-PBA/Dex@TAF. The outer Hep-PBA layer accumulates at the lesion sites by targeting P-selectin on the inflamed pulmonary endothelium. In the weakly acidic local microenvironment, boronate-ester bonds break, releasing Hep-PBA for local anticoagulation. The exposed Dex@TAF core is internalized by macrophages through the recognition between tannic acid and toll-like receptor 4. Subsequently, intracellular metal-polyphenol networks are disassembled. Relying on the proton sponge effect, dexamethasone escapes from lysosomes and is released into the cytoplasm, whereas reactive oxygen species are eliminated via the Fe2+/Fe3+ redox cycle. The released dexamethasone activates glucocorticoid receptors and suppresses proinflammatory transcription, further reducing neutrophil activation and neutrophil extracellular trap production. This synergistic regulation blocks the inflammation-thrombosis cascade by alleviating platelet activation and endothelial injury. In a mouse model of acute lung injury complicated by thrombosis, this nanoplatform markedly alleviated cytokine storms, preserved the integrity of the lung tissue structure, and inhibited microthrombus formation. candidates.abstract: HER2, an ERBB2-encoded receptor tyrosine kinase, regulates cell growth and survival. HER2 overexpression or ERBB2 amplification can promote tumor growth and is used to identify cancers that may benefit from HER2-targeted therapies. However, the functional consequences of sequence variants are difficult to predict when they occur outside known functional sites. Cysteine-introducing variants pose a challenge because a new cysteine can either form an abnormal bond directly or disrupt an existing disulfide and change which interactions are possible. HER2 W452C variant provides a case study of this problem because it introduces a cysteine outside the canonical dimerization interface but near a native extracellular disulfide. We used structural modeling, molecular dynamics, protein-protein docking, and cell-based analysis to test how W452C could alter receptor organization. Direct C452-C452 pairing between HER2 receptors was consistently difficult to accommodate without severe receptor overlap. We therefore examined a conditional state in which the native disulfide was reorganized, leaving another cysteine available for intermolecular interaction. This state increased ectodomain flexibility and accommodated alternative cysteine-mediated contacts. Explicit-bond refinement showed that selected C452-C504 arrangements remained structurally compatible after covalent disulfide formation. In cells, W452C increased a DTT-sensitive high-molecular-weight HER2-containing species, supporting altered disulfide-dependent association. Together, these findings support a mechanism in which an introduced cysteine alters receptor organization by reorganizing the local disulfide network rather than simply forming a new bond itself. More broadly, they illustrate how structural analysis can reveal molecular consequences of genetic variants that are not apparent from sequence position alone and thereby inform precision-medicine variant interpretation.

candidates.authors: Ropón-Palacios G, Crespi LGF, Martins IBS, Rocchia W, de Araujo AS
candidates.abstract: Dengue pathogenesis depends on a conformational rearrangement of the envelope glycoprotein (pE) induced by low pH. However, how pH and temperature cooperate to destabilize the dimeric form of the pE, a fundamental step that enables the formation of the fusion-active trimer, remains unclear. Here, we investigate this synergy for Dengue serotypes of greatest medical relevance, DENV-2 and DENV-3. All–atom molecular dynamics simulations were performed on the microsecond scale, at 28 °C, 37 °C, and 40 °C under pH 5, 6, and 7 using CHARMM36m force fields and complemented by extended coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations for the DENV-2 system at 37 °C and pH 5, and for the DENV-3 system at 28 °C and pH 5, and at 37 °C and pH 7. Acidification appears to amplify this effect in a serotype–specific manner: in our simulations DENV-2 required pH 5, while DENV-3 responded at pH 6. Additionally, distance and principal component analyses revealed an asymmetric dissociation pathway, termed the “compensatory embrace”, observed in both all-atom and coarse-grained models. Structural analyses further highlighted the differences in histidine distribution between the serotypes. Moreover, interaction mapping at 37 °C identified candidate interfacial contacts that may act as pH-sensitive latches, maintaining stability at pH 7 but breaking upon acidification. Collectively, these results suggest a potential hierarchy of physicochemical triggers that may contribute to the conversion of dimer into fusion-competent monomers. These interfacial hotspots and the “compensatory embrace” constitute structurally informed targets that, pending validation under native virion conditions, may guide the rational design of antivirals and immunogens, underscoring the value of long-time scale molecular dynamics simulations as a hypothesis-generating tool in drug discovery.

candidates.title: Comparative analysis of photocatalytic, enzymatic, and chemical approaches to identify canonical and noncanonical surfaceomes
candidates.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
candidates.journal_abbrev: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
candidates.authors: Ho WW, Chen Y, Slezak T, Zginnyk O, Peters-Clarke TM, Schaefer K, Kossiakoff AA, Leung KK, Wells JA
candidates.abstract: SignificanceThe cell surface proteome is an important area of study for disease biology and intervention. Existing surfaceomics strategies based on small molecule chemistry have limited detection scope and poor temporal control, while those based on enzymatic radical generators induce oxidative stress at biologic temperatures where the surfaceome can remodel. Photocatalysis, akin to molecular photography, has emerged as a promising tool in proximity labeling proteomics but has yet to be applied broadly for unbiased surfaceomics. Here, we employ protein-agnostic photocatalysis to achieve high resolution, minimally perturbing snapshots of the cell surface. By systematic comparison of eight surfaceomics methods, we uncover large numbers of nonglycosylated and noncanonical cell surface proteins that comprise an emerging class of surface localized proteins.

candidates.title: Computational Design Strategies for Nanoscale 3D Auxetic Metastructures from DNA
candidates.authors: Seo S, Madhvacharyula AS, Swett AA, Li R, Du Y, Choi JH
candidates.abstract: Auxetic metamaterials exhibit negative Poisson’s ratio (NPR) behaviors due to their architecture of periodically arranged unit cells. Although mechanical metamaterials are well established at the macroscale, programmable auxetic units remain scarce at the nanoscale. DNA origami offers a promising platform to bridge this gap, but design principles for dynamically deformable 3D auxetic nanostructures remain largely unexplored. Here, we develop design strategies for such 3D auxetic metastructures built from wireframe DNA origami. As a model system, we use a 3D re-entrant triangular unit composed of double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) bundle edges connected by single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) joints. Using coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) and umbrella-sampling free-energy simulations, we examine how edge design and joint-connection schemes govern auxetic responses and the energetics of the structural transformation. Our results show that auxetic performance and deformation energetics emerge from the coupled effects of DNA bundle rigidity and connector mechanics at the joints. This study provides mechanistic insights and design guidelines for programmable auxetic motion and energetics in 3D DNA origami metamaterials, advancing the development of stimuli-responsive nanomechanical devices.

candidates.title: Coordination Chemistry of Boron Subphthalocyanine With BINOL Derivatives: Unexpected Oxidation to Oxa[4]Helicene and Properties of the Resulting Axially Coordinated Complexes Containing Oxa[4]Helicene and/or BINOL Derivatives
candidates.authors: Islam S, Asahi K, Nishikawa H, Tauchi D, Hasegawa M, Sugiura K
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTIn the course of our research on axially coordinated metalloporphyrinoids with stable bonding based on the hard and soft acid–base (HSAB) theory, we focused on boron subphthalocyanine because of the hard acid character of the boron(III) center. 1,1′‐Bi‐2‐naphthol (BINOL) was selected as an axial ligand to introduce chirality into the otherwise achiral subphthalocyanine. Surprisingly, treatment of unsubstituted BINOL with boron subphthalocyanine resulted in the formation of a complex coordinated to an oxa[4]helicene derivative formed via a ring‐closure reaction of BINOL. In contrast, treatment of the monomethyl ether of BINOL with boron subphthalocyanine afforded the expected axially coordinated complex. Based on several control experiments, we propose a reaction mechanism for the formation of the oxa[4]helicene involving coordination of BINOL, followed by deprotonation and racemization, and subsequent intramolecular ring‐closure via an ionic process. To characterize and elucidate the fundamental properties of the resulting complexes, single‐crystal x‐ray diffraction, NMR spectroscopy, UV–vis absorption spectroscopy, and electrochemical studies were carried out. Furthermore, we investigated the chirality‐derived properties of the complexes, and the chirality‐induced spin selectivity (CISS) effect was evaluated using magnetic conductive atomic force microscopy (mc‐AFM), revealing a large spin polarization.

candidates.title: Emodin attenuates CFA-induced inflammatory pain in association with suppression of the Cx3cl1/Cx3cr1/p38 MAPK signaling axis
candidates.authors: Zheng X, Dai J, Mao C, Zhang W, Huang J, Hu S
candidates.abstract: ObjectivesTo investigate the analgesic effect of emodin on Complete Freund’s Adjuvant (CFA)-induced inflammatory pain and to clarify the underlying molecular mechanism.MethodsEmodin was administered intraperitoneally or prophylactically to attenuate CFA-induced inflammatory pain. RNA-seq was performed to identify the biological functions of differentially expressed genes in mouse dorsal root ganglion (DRG) tissues. The expression levels of Cx3cl1/Cx3cr1 were evaluated by RT-qPCR, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence. Pharmacological and genetic approaches were employed to block Cx3cr1 and assess its effect on pain thresholds in CFA-treated mice. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was used to examine the infiltration of immune and inflammatory cells in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) tissues before and after emodin treatment. Following emodin treatment, the levels of p-p38/p38 in DRG tissues were determined by Western blotting, and the mRNA levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines Tnf-α, Il-1β, and Il-6 in DRG tissues were measured by RT-qPCR.ResultsBoth therapeutic and prophylactic administration of emodin effectively alleviated CFA-induced mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity. Emodin treatment suppressed the CFA-induced upregulation of Cx3cl1/Cx3cr1 mRNA and protein levels in the DRG. Pharmacological and genetic blockade of Cx3cr1 effectively attenuated CFA-induced hyperalgesia. In addition, emodin markedly inhibited p-p38/p38 protein expression in the DRG of mice with CFA-induced inflammatory pain, reduced immune cell infiltration in DRG tissues, and downregulated the levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines Tnf-α, Il-1β, and Il-6.ConclusionEmodin attenuated CFA-induced inflammatory pain in mice, an effect associated with reduced Cx3cl1/Cx3cr1 signaling, decreased p38 MAPK activation, diminished immune-cell infiltration in the DRG, and lower expression of the proinflammatory cytokines Tnf-α, Il-1β, and Il-6 in DRG tissue.

candidates.title: Engineering bacterial morphology through MreB remodeling enhances one-carbon metabolism for sustainable bioproduction
candidates.authors: Chen Y, Peng J, Guo L, Tan Z
candidates.abstract: The actin-like cytoskeletal protein MreB controls bacterial cell morphology, yet whether engineered modulation of MreB-associated architecture can improve microbial metabolism remains largely unexplored. Here, we established a chemical-genetic platform in Escherichia coli combining an engineered MreB variant (A53R) that remodels cellular morphology with A22-mediated perturbation of MreB dynamics. MreB(A53R) reshaped cell morphology and engaged an RpoE-Cra-GadE regulatory network associated with cellular adaptation, which remodeled electron transport, redirected carbon flux toward NADPH-generating pathways, and reduced intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS). Consequently, engineered strains exhibited enhanced formaldehyde tolerance and efficient assimilation of methanol and other C1 substrates. Acute A22 treatment recapitulated the morphological alteration but failed to induce metabolic rewiring, revealing a two-stage adaptive response involving immediate physical adaptation associated with cell envelope reinforcement and long-term transcription-dependent metabolic adaptation to persistent morphological remodeling. The analogous V45R mutation in the native methylotroph Bacillus methanolicus partially recapitulated the improved C1 utilization phenotype, supporting the transferability of MreB-based morphological engineering. Collectively, these findings establish MreB-mediated morphological engineering as a strategy to couple cellular architecture with central carbon and redox metabolism and provide a framework for engineering robust microbial chassis for C1 bioconversion.

candidates.title: Euchromatin forms condensed domains with short active regions on the surface
candidates.authors: Paggi JM, Long LY, Zhang B
candidates.abstract: The three-dimensional organization of enhancers and promoters at nucleosome resolution remains poorly resolved, limiting our understanding of the structural basis of transcriptional regulation. Here we developed a simulation framework that leverages region-capture micro-C (RCMC) contact maps to infer conformational ensembles of megabase-scale regions at nucleosome resolution. A key component of this framework is a micro-C balancing strategy that identifies variation in contact density. The simulations reproduce pairwise distance distributions measured via chromatin tracing and contain packing domains and nucleosome clutches as observed in imaging studies. The inferred structures reveal a striking departure from the classical view of euchromatin as uniformly open. Instead, euchromatin generally forms condensed domains with comparable densities but smaller sizes than heterochromatin domains. Kilobase-scale regions at promoters and enhancers often protrude from these condensed domains, becoming highly accessible. This arrangement effectively compartmentalizes regulatory elements from the surrounding chromatin, facilitating protein binding and enhancer–promoter communication.

candidates.title: Evaluation of Physics-Based Pose Prediction and the Role of Receptor Flexibility in a Community Antiviral Blind Challenge
candidates.journal: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
candidates.authors: Khoualdi AF, Clark F, Horton JT, Cole DJ
candidates.abstract: Prediction of protein–ligand binding modes is a key step in computer-aided drug design, since incorrect pose prediction inevitably limits the achievable accuracy of downstream physics-based affinity predictions. The ASAP-Polaris-OpenADMET antiviral competition was launched in 2025 as a means to prospectively test computational methods across a range of measurements that guide early prioritization during a drug discovery campaign including pose prediction. Here, we describe our two open-source, physics-based entries to the pose prediction challenge, which are based on templated molecular growth with hybrid machine learning/molecular mechanics interatomic potentials. We show that our approach was among the top-performing physics-based methods, and with a retrospective change to the workflow to make greater use of the training data as templates, we obtain a success rate of 74% across SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV main protease target protein structures. Finally, we investigate the importance of receptor side-chain flexibility on retrospective performance. We find that building poses against an ensemble of feasible side-chain conformers is useful in generating improved binding poses but that the tested scoring functions are unable to successfully pick out native structures from the generated ensemble.

candidates.title: Evolutionarily diverged on-switch for actin assembly in fungal endocytosis
candidates.authors: Sebellin J, Kandiyoth FB, Bagyashree VT, Picco A, Carvalho N, Hakala M, Rivier-Cordey AS, Michelot A, Toret CP, Kaksonen M
candidates.abstract: Branched actin networks provide force for endocytic vesicle formation, yet what triggers their assembly in budding yeast has remained unknown. Sebellin et al. identify Ldb17 as the endocytic actin on-switch, controlled by the coat protein Sla1 through separate recruitment and activation steps, a regulation lost in fission yeast.

candidates.title: HAP40 functions as a proteostasis regulator by controlling huntingtin interactions and its release into the extracellular space
candidates.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
candidates.journal_abbrev: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
candidates.authors: Silva Ramos E, Boeddrich A, Haenig C, Trepte P, Ammar O, Secker C, Popp O, Ivanov A, Beetz S, Roth L, Papawassiliou RM, Hernandez Jeppesen LC, Wallenfang T, Keith B, Harding RJ, Schindler F, Koudelka T, Scharek N, Zenkner M, Neuendorf N, Golusik S, Mertins P, Piazza I, Schnoegl S, Wanker EE
candidates.abstract: SignificanceHuntingtin (HTT) interacts with thousands of proteins, including Huntingtin-associated protein 40 (HAP40), which stabilizes its conformation. How HAP40 influences HTT abundance and function is not fully defined. Here, using HAP40 knockout models, we report that HAP40 is an obligate binding partner which fundamentally controls HTT behavior. HAP40 not only alters HTT conformation but also defines its subcellular localization and protein interaction profile. Loss of HAP40 impairs autophagic protein degradation, triggers massive transcriptional dysregulation and leads to compensatory secretion of a large ~205 kDa mutant HTT fragment into the extracellular space through Golgi-associated pathways. These findings establish HAP40 as a proteostasis regulator that is required to stabilize canonical HTT interactions and mitigate mutant HTT proteotoxicity.

candidates.title: Harmine selectively enhances human beta cell identity markers and function via protein kinase A pathways
candidates.authors: Wang P, Kumar K, Lambertini L, Liu H, Wood O, Chen S, Pillard A, Scott DK, Paulo JA, Gygi SP, Khamrui S, Mueller S, Garcia-Ocana A, Karakose E, Lazarus MB, DeVita RJ, Stewart AF
candidates.abstract: Aims/hypothesisHarmine and other small-molecule inhibitors of the kinase, dual tyrosine-regulated kinase 1A (DYRK1A), induce human beta cells to replicate and regenerate in vitro and in vivo and are effective at reversing diabetes in animal models. In addition to its beta cell proliferative and regenerative effects, which result from inhibition of DYRK1A (‘Target 1’), harmine also induces expression of essential transcription factors and other genes involved in beta cell identity and function, exemplified by PDX1, MAFA, NKX6.1, MAFB, SIX3, SLC2A2, ENTPD3 and others. Harmine also rapidly enhances glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in vitro and in vivo. These beta cell identity-enhancing effects are not due to DYRK1A inhibition. We hypothesise that they reflect interactions of harmine with a second target (‘Target 2’). We aimed to identify Target 2.MethodsWe performed an in-depth analysis of multiple different small-molecule inhibitors of DYRK1A in human pancreatic islets using gene expression, single-cell RNA-seq, proliferation, immunocytochemistry of beta cell transcription factors and identity markers, and solid-phase precipitation combined with proteomics.ResultsAll small-molecule DYRK1A inhibitors studied (harmine, 2-2c, 5-IT, INDY, leucettine, CC-401, GNF4877) induced human beta cell proliferation via inhibition of DYRK1A. In contrast, silencing DYRK1A had no effect on beta cell transcription factors and identity markers. Further, harmine, 2-2c and 5-IT but not INDY, leucettine, CC-401 or GNF4877 enhanced expression of beta cell phenotypic markers. The enhanced expression of beta cell identity markers resulted from an unexpected activation by harmine of an as-yet unidentified Target 2 that activates the protein kinase A (PKA) pathway.Conclusions/interpretationThese findings make it clear that all DYRK1A inhibitors are not interchangeable. Those that drive both beta cell proliferation and identity/function will likely be preferable for diabetes therapy. Unravelling the mechanisms controlling the complex harmine–PKA–DYRK1A interactome will provide fruitful ground for future studies.Graphical Abstract Supplementary InformationThe online version of this article (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00125-026-06857-5) contains peer-reviewed but unedited supplementary material.

candidates.title: Heterojunction nanozyme achieve highly efficient antibacterial by cuproptosis-like death and ferroptosis-like death
candidates.authors: Wang W, Zhu R, Gui H, Jin X, Wei X, Wang X
candidates.abstract: Metal-ion-mediated lethal pathways offers a highly potent strategy for antibacterial treatments. However, relying on single-pathway mechanisms often fails to overwhelm bacterial antioxidant defenses, reducing antibacterial efficacy. This study designed a heterojunction nanozyme (Cu2O/Fe2O3) that induces ferroptosis-like death and copper-mediated metabolic toxicity exhibiting cuproptosis-like features, achieving highly effective antibacterial treatment. Computational chemistry analysis indicates that the Cu2O/Fe2O3 heterointerface establishes a built-in electric field through spontaneous interfacial electron transfer, thereby enhancing its peroxidase (POD)-like activity. Within the acidic bacterial microenvironment, Cu2O/Fe2O3 catalyzes the generation of large amounts of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and releases metal ions, inducing and amplifying ferroptosis-like death, which disrupts the function of ETC enzymes by attacking iron–sulfur clusters. Concurrently, copper ions disrupt the redox balance by depleting bacillithiol (BSH), indirectly increasing bacterial susceptibility and promoting ferroptosis-like death. Furthermore, the accumulation of copper ions triggers severe metabolic impairments that biochemically resemble the cuproptosis cascade, which disrupts key enzymes of the TCA cycle and impairs the synthesis of electron donors (NADH and FADH2), thereby cutting off the supply of substrates to ETC at the upstream stage. Overall, this study demonstrates that triggering bimetallic ion-mediated metabolic disruptions induces an energy crisis in bacteria, providing a reference for multimodal antibacterial strategies.

candidates.title: Identification and validation of candidate biomarkers associated with mitochondrial metabolism in diabetic foot
candidates.authors: Li H, Ning Y, Lu C, Zhang Y, Yan S, Chang W, Jin H, Tian Q, Shi Y, Qiao M, Zhang Y, Dong H
candidates.abstract: BackgroundAlthough the precise regulatory mechanisms underlying diabetic foot (DF) remain incompletely understood, increasing evidence suggests that mitochondrial metabolism may be involved in DF progression. The study aimed to identify and validate candidate biomarkers associated with mitochondrial metabolism in DF.MethodsTranscriptome sequencing data from 12 DF and 18 control tissue samples were analyzed together with 1,234 mitochondrial metabolism-related genes (MMRGs), which were obtained from MSigDB by integrating curated gene sets directly associated with mitochondrial metabolic processes. First, overlapping genes between MMRGs and DEGs between DF and control samples were used as candidate genes. Then, candidate biomarkers were identified using PPI network construction, two machine learning algorithms, and ROC curve analysis. Next, based on the candidate biomarkers, functional enrichment, immune infiltration, regulatory network, compound prediction, as well as molecular docking analyses were undertaken. Finally, to explore the expression of candidate biomarkers in clinical samples, the reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) was performed.ResultsGPAT3 and PTGS2 were identified as mitochondrial metabolism-associated candidate biomarkers for DF, with area under the curve values of 0.963 and 0.958, respectively. Functional enrichment analysis showed that multiple pathways were significantly enriched by both GPAT3 and PTGS2, such as ribosome and Leishmania infection. GPAT3 had the strongest positive and negative correlations with neutrophils and resting CD4 memory T cells, respectively. In contrast, PTGS2 exhibited the strongest negative connection with M1 macrophages and the strongest positive correlation with neutrophils. Subsequently, multiple transcription factors (TFs) were found to co-target GPAT3 and PTGS2, such as BRD4 and NR0B1. Moreover, compound prediction analysis identified several compounds potentially associated with these biomarkers, such as lipopolysaccharides and cisplatin. The binding free energy between PTGS2 and tetradecanoylphorbol acetate was − 8.2 kcal/mol, while the binding free energy between GPAT3 and cyclosporine was − 10.4 kcal/mol, according to molecular docking data. Finally, the expression levels of GPAT3 and PTGS2 were significantly different in clinical samples.ConclusionGPAT3 and PTGS2 were identified as candidate biomarkers associated with mitochondrial metabolism in DF, providing molecular clues for further investigation of DF pathogenesis and potential intervention strategies.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12902-026-02445-1.

candidates.title: Identification of TMEM263 as an ER-resident protein that controls early stages of lipid droplet biogenesis
candidates.authors: Yalci K, Chala N, Moss J, MacDonald C, Zakrzewski P, Smith P, Sevil R, Willoughby L, Wonklyn S, Andrews T, Hammond CL, Corey RA, Carroll B
candidates.abstract: Cell and organismal growth is controlled not only by the availability of nutrients, but also the ability to dynamically sense and respond to changes in metabolic demand. We have identified a protein, TMEM263 (also known as C12orf23) as a mechanistic link between growth and lipid metabolism. TMEM263 was discovered in a screen as an ER-resident protein, and we have characterised its role as both necessary and sufficient for lipid droplet formation. TMEM263 has two transmembrane domains that fold into a dynamic alpha hairpin which are essential for its localisation to the ER and to support lipid droplet accumulation. Functionally, we propose that TMEM263 can interact with and support the condensation of neutral lipids in a bilayer to promote lipid droplet formation and growth. Consistently, loss of TMEM263 in cells and in zebrafish significantly impairs lipid droplet accumulation. Loss of TMEM263 protein function in vivo is associated with organismal growth defects and proportional dwarfism and our study provides a mechanistic understanding linking these phenotypes to impaired lipid droplet biology.

candidates.title: Light-activated viologen-based metal-covalent organic framework sprayable hydrogel for accelerated healing of infected skin wounds
candidates.journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology
candidates.authors: Feng LJ, Tong JL, Xie QX, Wen MN, Ma XZ, Zang Y, Zhong JR, Yao J, Li XM, Zhao B, Tang P
candidates.abstract: Bacterial resistance and recurrent infection remain major challenges for infected wound healing. Antibacterial photodynamic therapy (aPDT) features excellent spatiotemporal control and low risk of inducing bacterial resistance, making it a promising antibacterial modality. However, many photosensitizers used in wound therapy are photounstable, bind weakly to bacteria, and generate insufficient reactive oxygen species (ROS). We developed a viologen-functionalized metal-covalent organic framework (Vio-MCOF) by covalently embedding viologen units into the MCOF framework, and integrated this material into a sprayable, ionically crosslinked sodium alginate hydrogel. In this system, viologen units serve as electron mediators and work cooperatively with the copper-cluster active sites to suppress charge recombination and may increase ROS production under simulated solar light. The positive charge of the viologen units promotes electrostatic binding of Vio-MCOF to negatively charged bacterial membranes, improving its photodynamic antibacterial performance. In vitro experiments showed that Vio-MCOF at 200 μg mL-1 achieved a bactericidal rate of over 99% against S. aureus after 30 min of simulated solar light irradiation. In vivo experiments demonstrated that the Vio-MCOF hydrogel reduced bacterial colonization in infected wounds, suppressed TNF-α and IL-6 expression, alleviated inflammation, and promoted angiogenesis and collagen deposition, leading to accelerated wound healing. Collectively, the sprayable Vio-MCOF hydrogel holds promise as an antibiotic-free dressing for infected skin wounds.

candidates.title: Lipid-sensing GPR183-KRAS signaling mediates TH17 autoimmunity and identifies fluvoxamine repurposing in uveitis
candidates.authors: Zhang C, Liu X, Xu N, Chen H, Gao Y, Gu C, Shen X, Wu J, Lu X, Zhang P, He Y, Xu Z, Su W
candidates.abstract: Autoimmune uveitis (AU) is a leading cause of irreversible blindness driven by pathogenic T helper 17 (TH17) cell–mediated inflammation, yet current therapies are limited by efficacy and side effects, with immunometabolic mechanisms remaining poorly defined. By integrating single-cell RNA sequencing and multilayered metabolomic profiling in patients with AU and experimental AU models, we identified the lipid-sensing G protein–coupled receptor GPR183 as a key immunometabolic regulator in pathogenic CD4+ T cells. Upon activation, GPR183 modulates intracellular signaling via suppression of cyclic adenosine monophosphate–cAMP-dependent protein kinase activity and promotion of son-of-sevenless–dependent KRAS activation, which in turn elicits copper overload–induced mitochondrial oxidative stress, structural impairment, and metabolic rewiring toward glycolysis, thereby promoting TH17 cell pathogenicity. For clinical translation, virtual screening of Food and Drug Administration–approved drugs coupled with molecular docking and microscale thermophoresis validation identified fluvoxamine (FLV) as a direct GPR183 antagonist. In in vivo and in vitro uveitis and colitis models, FLV attenuated GPR183-KRAS signaling, dampened pathogenic TH17 cell responses, and alleviated tissue inflammation. These findings delineate a unique GPR183-KRAS–mitochondrial damage axis governing TH17-driven autoimmunity and support repurposing FLV as a translatable therapeutic approach for AU and other autoimmune inflammatory disorders.
