candidates.title: Membrane damage induces TagQ/TagR complex-mediated H1-T6SS assembly in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
candidates.authors: Kolesnikov M, Berneiser K, Prakash P, Basler M
candidates.abstract: The type VI secretion system (T6SS) is a large macromolecular complex crucial for inter-bacterial competition. Its expression and localization are tightly regulated, with the anti-bacterial H1-T6SS in Pseudomonas aeruginosa assembling in response to membrane damage. While several proteins are known to regulate this response, the mechanism remains unknown. Here, we use biochemical approaches to show formation of a complex between the membrane lipoprotein TagQ and the periplasmic protein TagR. Furthermore, Co-IP and in silico modeling indicates TagQ/R complex interactions with PpkA, likely dimerizing the kinase to initiate a phosphorylation cascade leading to H1-T6SS assembly. Mass spectrometry analysis of phosphorylated proteins in P. aeruginosa shows that PpkA does not have any targets outside of the previously reported Fha1, suggesting the sensor module acts exclusively to regulate T6SS assembly. Our work reveals the functional basis of the TagQR-PpkA signaling pathway and links membrane damage to localized H1-T6SS assembly, which is critical for efficient retaliation during inter-bacterial interactions.

candidates.title: Modular Triethylene Glycol Decouples Antimicrobial Potency from Cytotoxicity in Membrane-Active Drugs
candidates.authors: Seewald M, Stamen M, Li J, Engelkamp S, Behnke JS, Lucassen R, Borowick K, Weilburg M, Wycisk V, Fielitz T, Wu TC, Hartlieb M, Schaumburg F, Bockmühl D, Raisch T, Urner LH
candidates.abstract: Cationic membrane-active drugs are an important focus of antibiotic research, yet their potential is often limited by poor selectivity. Here, we establish steric protection of cations by modular triethylene glycol as a chemical design framework to decouple antimicrobial potency from cytotoxicity. Using antipsychotics, a class of widely prescribed membrane-active drugs, we show that lipophilicity and rigidity jointly govern antimicrobial potency and mammalian cell cytotoxicity. Membrane perturbation emerged as a key determinant of bioactivity and revealed physicochemical windows that decouple antimicrobial potency and cytotoxicity. Our findings spotlight octanol as a design motif for steric protection of cations that emerged from systematic tuning of side chain lipophilicity and mimics a known metabolite motif. As exemplified with the model drug chlorpromazine, this modification can maintain water solubility, improve membrane engagement, reduce mammalian cell cytotoxicity, enhance antibacterial potency, and amplify polymyxin amplification across Gram-negative bacteria, including drug-resistant clinical isolates. Our findings indicate that membrane remodeling associated with polymyxin resistance in Escherichia coli correlates with a collateral vulnerability to cationic amphiphiles, suggesting a physicochemically tractable consequence of resistance. These findings establish a chemical design framework for small-molecule cationic amphiphiles with improved physicochemical properties, membrane engagement, and bioactivity that can be difficult to achieve by traditional alkylation.

candidates.title: NIR-responsive carbon monoxide nanoplatform for synergistic antibacterial and anti-inflammatory therapy of refractory keratitis and biofilm-infected wounds
candidates.authors: Han Y, Deng K, Chen R, Chen F, Yao K, Ye Y, Du Z, Shentu X
candidates.abstract: Drug-resistant bacterial biofilms hinder the treatment of persistent infections by limiting drug penetration and reducing bacterial susceptibility through their dense extracellular matrix and active signaling networks. Herein, we developed a near-infrared (NIR) light-responsive, bacteria-targeting nanoplatform, termed UCMSP-CL, for localized carbon monoxide (CO) delivery and biofilm eradication. UCMSP-CL disrupts biofilm architecture and adheres to bacteria through electrostatic interactions and enzyme-substrate recognition. Subsequent NIR irradiation triggers local CO release, which induces severe bacterial metabolic exhaustion by inhibiting the bacterial respiratory chain, depleting ATP and compromising membrane integrity, while exerting potent anti-inflammatory effects. In murine models of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) keratitis and infected skin wounds, NIR-irradiated UCMSP-CL markedly reduced bacterial burden, promoted biofilm clearance, alleviated local inflammation, and accelerated tissue repair. These findings establish a controllable platform that couples antibacterial and anti-inflammatory activities, offering a potential strategy for treating biofilm-associated and drug-resistant infections.

candidates.title: On the limits of marginal protein folding stability: methodological goals and drawbacks
candidates.authors: Ferreiro D, Zoni V, Arenas M
candidates.abstract: ContextWhy do proteins remain at the edge of stability rather than evolving toward maximal thermodynamic robustness? Can we trust the computational methods that inform about when and how stability falls off that edge? Marginal stability, the confinement of protein folding free energies to a window of approximately 5–15 kcal/mol, is broadly observed in biophysics, and its mechanistic causes, involving evolutionary and biophysical properties, remain under debate and require accurate predictions. In this regard, protein folding stability is currently predicted using both traditional structure-based homology-modeling methods and modern sequence-based deep-learning methods. However, comparisons among these methodologies remain scarce.MethodsUsing four viral proteins of biomedical interest and considering that rapidly evolving viral proteins provide a useful system for understanding thermodynamic tolerance under the competing demands of structural integrity and adaptive flexibility, we compared predicted protein stability from both approaches across independent random mutational trajectories and naturally occurring sequence variants available in public databases. The results showed a general methodological impasse. As random mutations accumulated, structure-based methods predicted a progressive decline in stability toward collapse, a pattern driven by the enforced conservation of protein structure. In contrast, sequence-based methods failed as sequences moved into uncharted regions of parameter space. Together, protein stability landscapes predicted using current computational approaches are inherently shaped by technical limitations, leading to uncertainty in the evaluation of marginal stability and stability changes associated with biological processes.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s00894-026-07034-6.

candidates.title: Overexpression of the endogenous diguanylate cyclase gene dgcS enhances biofilm formation by Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 on electrodes
candidates.authors: Iwanami N, Matsumoto A, Yamamoto R, Tomita K, Kouzuma A, Watanabe K
candidates.abstract: In microbial electrochemical technologies, Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 efficiently generates electric current via biofilm formation on electrodes. A previous study demonstrated that the deletion of the diguanylate cyclase gene dgcS inhibits biofilm formation on electrodes and current generation in MR-1. However, the molecular mechanisms by which dgcS expression and subsequent cyclic dimeric guanosine monophosphate (c-di-GMP) signaling affect these processes remain unexplored. Here, we investigated the effects of dgcS overexpression on current generation, electrode-associated biofilm formation, and the intracellular concentration of cyclic AMP (cAMP), a second messenger that induces the expression of extracellular electron transfer (EET)-related genes in MR-1, to examine the potential coordinated regulation of intracellular c-di-GMP and cAMP levels. In an electrochemical flow cell (EFC), the dgcS-overexpressing (dgcS-OE) strain exhibited significantly higher intracellular c-di-GMP concentrations than the vector control (VC) strain, forming more biomass-rich biofilms on the electrode and generating higher current. However, current generation normalized to electrode-associated biomass did not differ significantly between the dgcS-OE and VC strains, suggesting that dgcS overexpression did not increase EET activity per biomass. Moreover, intracellular cAMP levels were not significantly different between the dgcS-OE and VC strains, and the transcription levels of adenylate cyclase (cAMP synthase) genes and EET-related genes in the dgcS-OE strain tended to be reduced to 0.3- to 0.6-fold of those in the VC strain. Collectively, these findings suggest that dgcS overexpression and the associated elevation of intracellular c-di-GMP levels enhance the electrogenic performance of MR-1 primarily by promoting biofilm development on electrodes, while weakly repressing the transcription of genes related to cAMP signaling.

candidates.title: PanRes: a database of latent and acquired antimicrobial resistance allowing 3D-based protein homology search
candidates.authors: Vojtková M, Baltušis M, Martiny HM, Baral A, Pyrounakis N, Beleon A, Freitag R, Pico-Tomàs A, Kaas RS, Petersen TN, Munk P
candidates.abstract: AbstractMotivationAntimicrobial resistance databases are central to genomic surveillance, but resistance determinants remain distributed across resources with different scopes, structures, and annotations.ResultsWe developed PanRes, a curated resistance database of 11 717 genes integrating acquired and latent determinants of antibiotic, biocide, and metal resistance within a unified ontology. We predicted representative protein structures and clustered them by structural similarity, grouping proteins into 505 high-confidence structurally conserved clusters coherent despite sequence divergence. Their structure-guided alignments were used to build Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) for remote homology search. In seven wastewater metagenomes from five European cities, PanRes 3D-based HMMs expanded detection beyond what was possible with BLAST, with 35.3% of retained hits identified only by the HMMs and generally showing greater divergence from known proteins. For beta-lactamases, several proteins retained beta-lactamase-like folds and catalytic geometry despite weak sequence similarity.Availability and implementationPanRes is available through an interactive web platform (https://panres.rambio.dk/), a structure-informed resource for exploring the whole resistome. The database, HMM profiles, and ontology are available at Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.22876216).

candidates.title: Raman Optical Activity as a Tool to Monitor Polynucleotide Conformation in Solutions
candidates.authors: Para Kkadan MS, Kapitán J, Kessler J, Zapletal O, Andrushchenko V, Bouř P
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTThe reactivity and function of biopolymers depend on their structure and flexibility. There is a limited number of methods that can be used for their studies in solutions. Among them, Raman optical activity (ROA) provides excellent sensitivity to conformational changes. So far, ROA studies of nucleic acid systems are relatively rare because of the complexity of these molecules and difficulties in interpretation of the spectra. To explore the link between spectral shapes and the structure, and to advance the experimental and computational methodologies, we measured Raman and ROA spectra of four oligonucleotides (polyA, polyC, polyG, and polyU) in a wide wavenumber range. Molecular dynamics (MD) and density functional theory (DFT) were used for the spectra simulations. Temperature‐dependent vibrational spectral changes are consistent with melting curves obtained from electronic circular dichroism (ECD). The results show that the spectra well‐reflect molecular geometry, including changes caused by temperature variation. Comparison of theoretical and experimental Raman and ROA intensities appears as a convenient way to validate and potentially develop MD force fields; the RNA.Shaw force field provided results superior to the RNA.OL3 one. The combined spectroscopic and computational methodology thus can be used as a powerful means to study solution properties of nucleic acids.

candidates.title: Sedative Potential of L (+)‐Tartaric Acid: Behavioral Evidence With In Silico Insights Into Possible GABAergic Interaction
candidates.authors: Bithi SA, Chakrabarty A, Akter K, Saha CK, Alshahrani MY, Hossain MA, Mia E, Yana NT, Ajmee A, Mandal P, Al Hasan MS, Islam MT
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACTPurposeInsomnia is a prevalent neurological disorder often caused by stress, anxiety, and imbalances in the GABAergic system. Although benzodiazepines like diazepam (DZP) are commonly prescribed, their long‐term use is associated with adverse effects, including dependence and impaired coordination. Therefore, there is growing interest in natural alternatives with safer pharmacological profiles.MethodThis study aimed to investigate the sedative‐like potential of L (+)‐tartaric acid (LTA), a naturally occurring organic acid, through both in vivo and in silico approaches targeting the γ‐aminobutyric acid A (GABAA) receptor. Sedative‐like activity was evaluated in Swiss albino mice using thiopental sodium‐induced sleeping time, open‐field, and rotarod tests.FindingsLTA significantly reduced sleep latency and prolonged sleep duration in a dose‐dependent manner, with the higher dose (240 mg/kg) producing a more pronounced effect. Co‐administration of LTA with DZP further enhanced thiopental‐induced hypnosis. In the open‐field test, LTA reduced locomotor and exploratory activities, as evidenced by decreases in square crossings, rearing, and grooming behaviors. Rotarod assessment demonstrated a dose‐dependent reduction in motor coordination and neuromuscular performance, although the impairment remained less pronounced than that produced by DZP at the lower tested dose. Molecular docking revealed lower binding affinity than DZP but demonstrated multiple hydrogen‐bond (HB) interactions with key amino acid (AA) residues of the GABAA receptor, suggesting a potentially stable receptor interaction.ConclusionCollectively, the behavioral and computational findings indicate that LTA possesses sedative‐like properties and may modulate GABAergic neurotransmission. Further mechanistic, pharmacokinetic, and electrophysiological studies are required to clarify its precise mode of action and therapeutic potential.

candidates.title: Serum albumin maintains Wnt3a water solubility and activity
candidates.authors: Yeo JH, Chae J, Kwon SS, Han J, Kusen I, Lim JY, Lee H, Kim H, Haam S, Cheong JH, Kim T, Moon SJ, Jung YO, Lee J, Kim CH
candidates.abstract: Wnt proteins regulate adult tissue homeostasis and repair by driving stem cell self-renewal and differentiation. High-performance Wnt preparations have enormous therapeutic potential, especially alongside various stem cell technologies. Currently, a major limitation of most Wnt preparations is that they inevitably require fetal bovine serum (FBS) or detergents to maintain Wnt solubility and activity. Recently, afamin (AFM) was identified as a serum factor that solubilizes Wnt3a in conditioned media (CM), obviating the requirement for animal sera. Here, we show that serum albumin (SA) helps maintain the activity and stability of AFM-solubilized Wnt3a in CM, likely through a stabilizing effect. We further demonstrate, using test-tube assays, that SA alone efficiently solubilizes purified Wnt3a (pWnt3a) independently of AFM. This approach enables the conversion of conventional detergent-solubilized pWnt3a (CHAPS–pWnt3a) into SA–pWnt3a through dialysis-mediated detergent removal. Together, these findings define a simple and robust SA-based strategy for preserving Wnt3a activity, addressing a long-standing challenge in both experimental and therapeutic settings.

candidates.title: StSIRT1 regulates potato dormancy through deacetylation of peroxidase-like 3 at K37
candidates.authors: Hu Q, Dong Y, Hu H, Xiang Y, Liu B, Wong TW, Ban Z, Luo Z, Li L
candidates.abstract: Plants have evolved sophisticated defense systems to synchronize growth with environmental fluctuations, including the adaptive strategy of dormancy, an important agronomic trait. Nevertheless, the role of posttranslational modification of nonhistone proteins in dormancy regulation remains elusive. Here, we report that sirtuin (StSIRT1)–mediated deacetylation of peroxidase (StPRX3) suppresses peroxidase activity, culminating in potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) dormancy release. The lysine deacetylase StSIRT1—suppressed by the dormancy regulator nicotinamide (NAM)—accumulates during dormancy release and negatively modulates StPRX3. Furthermore, lysine-37 (K37; K denotes lysine) in StPRX3 is essential for its direct interaction with StSIRT1. StSIRT1 interacts with StPRX3 to regulate the hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)–scavenging capacity of peroxidase by decreasing K37 acetylation levels. Notably, the StPRX3K37R (K37→arginine, K37R; R denotes arginine) mutant suppresses peroxidase activity, leading to accelerated potato dormancy release. Our findings uncover an StSIRT1-StPRX3 cascade in dormancy regulation that activates peroxidase and reduces H2O2 levels in potato, providing insights into the complex regulatory networks involved in dormancy.

candidates.title: Structure-Guided Design of a Subnanomolar Dengue Virus NS4B Inhibitor
candidates.journal: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
candidates.authors: Laorsatiankul P, Baig MH, Chen S, Hassan M, Khan PR, Ramanjaneyulu M, Joong KC, Seong JY, Dong JJ, Haider S
candidates.abstract: Dengue virus nonstructural protein 4B (NS4B) is an essential regulator of viral replication but remains structurally unresolved, limiting drug discovery. Here, we combine modeling, ligand-based design, and experimental validation to enable structure-guided inhibition of NS4B. Comparative models across all four serotypes reveal a conserved transmembrane binding pocket consistent with resistance mutations. Docking of JNJ-series inhibitors defines key interaction features that guide the development of predictive field-based 3D-QSAR models (R = 0.91, Q = 0.89). Prospective screening of bioisosteric and in-house compounds identifies BNJ-495 as a candidate broad-spectrum inhibitor with predicted activity across all four dengue serotypes. Experimental validation confirms potent activity against dengue virus serotype 2 (IC50 = 0.17 nM) with a high selectivity index (∼37,000). Conserved binding interactions across serotypes support broad-spectrum potential. This study establishes a general framework for targeting structurally elusive viral membrane proteins.

candidates.title: Sustainable biobased packaging via integrated robotics/machine learning workflow for improved postharvest preservation
candidates.authors: Li Y, Chen T, Ma P, Chung TC, Zhou B, Wu L, Golatkar AR, Mukta S, Little JM, Whitley HC, Luo Y, Wang Q, Curtzwiler G, Hu L, Li T, Chen PY
candidates.abstract: Reliance on petroleum-derived plastic packaging exacerbates environmental burdens and lacks intrinsic antimicrobial protection against food spoilage. While biobased materials offer a sustainable alternative, optimizing their formulations is hindered by vast component libraries, inefficient trial-and-error experimentation, and complex multiproperty requirements. Herein, we develop an integrated workflow combining robotic automation, machine learning predictions, density functional theory, and life cycle assessment to accelerate biobased packaging discovery. Leveraging data augmentation and ensemble modeling, we use a hierarchical neural network to predict ∼1 billion candidate formulations, balancing mechanical properties, optical transparency, and environmental footprint. The resulting biobased packaging demonstrates enhanced hydrostability, effective antimicrobial activity, and high barrier performance, significantly extending the shelf life of cucumbers and avocados. Last, we release a data-sharing platform featuring forward prediction, inverse design, and environmental impact functions to support community use. This integrative framework provides sustainable, antimicrobial packaging materials alternative to conventional plastic films.
